broad.text: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

problem_constrained.text: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

expert_context.text: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

hidden_target.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (x = 0), produced from high-purity elements, with an approximately 70% FCC-dominant FCC + ordered B2 dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
hidden_target.intervention: Zr was alloyed into AlCoCrFeNi2.1 at nominal x = 0.01, 0.05, and 0.1 (with x = 0 as the control), and the as-cast alloys were examined for phase/microstructure evolution, hardness, room-temperature compression, nanoindentation creep, and electrochemical corrosion.
hidden_target.conditions: Button ingots were made under Ar by cold-crucible/vacuum melting and remelted at least five times. Microhardness used a 0.981 N load for 15 s; room-temperature compression used 3 mm × 6 mm cylinders at 1 × 10^-3 s^-1 to strain 0.3. Nanoindentation creep used a 10 mN peak load, 100 s hold, and loading rates of 0.1, 1, and 5 mN/s. Corrosion testing was conducted after 30 min immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl using polarization from -0.8 to 1.5 V at 1 mV/s and EIS from 10^-2 to 10^4 Hz.
hidden_target.structural_mediator: Zr initially enters the FCC/B2 matrix and causes lattice distortion; at x >= 0.05, Ni- and Zr-rich Ni7Zr2 precipitates emerge at phase boundaries and bridge the FCC and B2 regions. Their morphology evolves from dispersed particles at low Zr to a discontinuous network at x = 0.05 and a coarse continuous network at x = 0.1, while the B2 fraction decreases. TEM of x = 0.1 also showed L12 precipitates in the FCC phase and nanoprecipitates in B2.
hidden_target.mechanism: Moderate Zr provides solid-solution strengthening through lattice distortion and dispersion/precipitation strengthening through fine, coherent or semi-coherent Ni7Zr2-related precipitates, impeding dislocations and grain-boundary sliding. Excess Zr coarsens and connects the Zr-rich phase, promotes Ni depletion from B2, reduces the B2 fraction, increases segregation and embrittlement, and therefore diminishes mechanical strengthening. For corrosion, the more continuous Zr-rich structure at x = 0.1 favors a stable, protective passive layer, plausibly including ZrO2, that blocks Cl- ingress; uneven intermediate precipitates can instead promote microgalvanic attack.
hidden_target.predicted_outcome: Relative to Zr-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1, moderate Zr addition—especially x = 0.05—should reduce creep deformation and increase hardness, yield strength, and compressive strength, whereas excessive Zr (x = 0.1) should lower room-temperature mechanical properties from the x = 0.05 optimum. In contrast, x = 0.1 should provide the best corrosion resistance through a more stable passive film.
hidden_target.baseline: The x = 0 as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy had an FCC + B2 lamellar structure, yield strength 705.1 ± 31.53 MPa, compressive strength 1182.7 ± 24.68 MPa, corrosion current density 0.09993 μA/cm2, pitting potential 320.27 mV, corrosion rate 0.0011621 mm/year, and charge-transfer resistance 2600 Ω·cm2.
hidden_target.boundary: The reported trends apply to the as-cast ZrxAlCoCrFeNi2.1 compositions x = 0, 0.01, 0.05, and 0.1 under the stated room-temperature mechanical/nanoindentation conditions and in 3.5 wt% NaCl. The mechanical optimum occurred at x = 0.05; increasing Zr to x = 0.1 reversed part of the strengthening benefit, while corrosion resistance was best at x = 0.1. Dislocation-dominated creep was most persistent at x = 0.05, whereas loading-rate changes altered the inferred mechanisms in the other alloys.
hidden_target.discriminating_measurement: XRD, SEM/EDS, and TEM/SAED identified phase and morphology changes; microhardness and room-temperature compression distinguished the mechanical optimum; nanoindentation creep displacement and the fitted stress exponent n distinguished creep resistance and mechanism; potentiodynamic polarization (Icorr, Ecorr, and Epit), EIS/Rct, and post-corrosion SEM/EDS distinguished corrosion resistance and passive-film stability.
hidden_target.actual_result: At x = 0.05, hardness peaked at 368.1 HV (about 18.7% above the Zr-free alloy), yield strength at 1048.7 ± 23.84 MPa (about 48.7% higher), and compressive strength at 1801.1 ± 28.70 MPa (about 52.2% higher). At x = 0.1 these fell to 865.9 ± 14.85 MPa and 1382.4 ± 13.56 MPa, respectively. At a 5 mN/s indentation loading rate, creep depth changed from 22.16 nm at x = 0 to 13.47 nm at x = 0.05, then rose to 18.36 nm at x = 0.1. The creep exponent exceeded 3 at 0.1 mN/s, and x = 0.05 retained n > 3 even at 5 mN/s, indicating dislocation creep and robust creep resistance. Corrosion resistance ranked x = 0.1 > x = 0.01 > x = 0.05 > x = 0; x = 0.1 had the lowest Icorr, 0.034197 μA/cm2, the highest Epit, 323.06 mV, a corrosion rate of 0.00039737 mm/year, and the highest Rct, 700,000 Ω·cm2.
